lesson.title: Replacing a Whole Circuit with One Source and One Resistor
lesson.summary: Thevenin's theorem shows how any linear resistive circuit, viewed from two terminals, behaves exactly like a single voltage source in series with a single resistor ,  this section sets up how to find that equivalent.
lesson.body:
Every time you analyze a circuit, you care about how it behaves at the two terminals where something else ,  a load ,  connects to it. Thevenin's theorem says that no matter how complicated the network behind those terminals is, as long as it's linear, it behaves exactly like one ideal voltage source in series with one resistor. You already know enough to find both pieces: the equivalent voltage is just the open-circuit voltage across the terminals (using Ohm's Law and KVL/KCL as usual), and the equivalent resistance is what you'd measure looking into the terminals with all independent sources turned off.

Take a 12V source feeding two 6Ω resistors in series, with the load connected across the second resistor. Remove the load: the open-circuit voltage divides evenly, giving 6V. Zero the source (short it) and look into the terminals: the two 6Ω resistors are now in parallel, giving 3Ω. So this whole circuit acts, from the load's point of view, like a 6V source with a 3Ω resistor in series.
